abstract: When observers interact with an object, each observer generates a different sequence of images. However, which image statistics underlie their perceptual judgments, and whether this self-generated visual input explains what they perceive, remain unclear. We analyzed the first-person recordings of a virtual-reality experiment in which 19 observers judged whether an object was metal or glass while exploring the object with the hand, with the head, with both, and without moving. The object was rendered in two shapes at five levels of physical metallicity and in four illumination environments; every observer saw every stimulus but did so through a different video. Simple image statistics pertaining to the object, to its relation with its surround and to the changes in these properties as the observer explored predicted observers' responses effectively. Critically, when observers disagreed with regard to the same stimulus, their own videos predicted which observer said metal more accurately than chance, and this observer-specific information emerged mainly in the few seconds that preceded the response. The predictive cues identified in this context included the coverage of the optic flow, contrast, highlight coverage, luminance, and the object's luminance and color relative to its surround; furthermore, their importance varied across observers. Thus, active exploration generates different visual evidence for different observers, and their material judgments follow the evidence that they generate.
